text:
This section examines Experiment L —
Aging, hybrid ideas, and

a positional surrogate from first
principles. Keep two questions separate:

does changing the order change the
measured outcome, and does

the proposed search method beat a matched
alternative at the

same distinct-evaluation budget? Methods:
elitist prism, aging evolution,

random, and a BANANAS-style ridge
surrogate using positional one-hot

features; later hybrid restart is
separated in Experiment N. Protocol:

four methods across three cached
landscapes, initially 15 seeds; 40-seed

verification on parity n=7; cap 500
distinct evaluations. Parity: aging

improved hit rate from roughly 48% to 78%,
but random

was about 75%; it fixed premature
convergence without creating locality.

Structured XOR n=6: elitist remained
faster, 18.5 versus 28.7 evaluations.

Positional surrogate: mild win on the LLM
landscape, inert on

parity. Decision: F D C-negative suggests
elitist search with a

matched or portfolio operator; F D C near
zero suggests

random or aging. Aging is a robust
default, not a

universal winner. Now read evidence panel
L-methods. The axes, units,

and sample are stated on screen. The
sample represented here

is 15 seeds. Raw observations remain
visible wherever the artifact

provides them. Censored observations stay
marked at the cap rather

than becoming invented hitting times, and
sampled landscapes leave

unobserved permutations blank. The
supported finding is: Parity: aging

improved hit rate from roughly 48% to 78%,
but random

was about 75%; it fixed premature
convergence without creating locality.

The broader claim not established here is:
The conclusion is

scoped to the recorded evaluator,
landscape, and budget. This evidence

changed the program as follows: Decision:
F D C-negative suggests

elitist search with a matched or portfolio
operator; F D

C near zero suggests random or aging. The
distinction is

part of the result. A large ordering
effect does not

automatically imply an evolutionary-search
advantage, and almost-sure

convergence does not promise practical
efficiency.
